Your allow list is not a boundary.

Claude Code evaluates permission rules in one order: deny, then ask, then allow. First match wins, and specificity does not change that order — so a deny rule cannot carry allowlist exceptions, and a broad allow cannot punch through a deny.

Two things people miss:

A Read deny also covers the file commands Claude runs in Bash — cat, head, tail, sed. And it blocks Edit and Write on the same path, so denying the read denies the rewrite.

Read(.env) and Read(**/.env) are the same rule. Bare filenames follow gitignore semantics and match at any depth.

captions.instagram:
Two schedulers. One slot. The database decides who owns it.

Metricool holds the batch already in its planner. Buffer got added for capacity. Neither knows about the other, and both publishing the same reel to the same account is not a bug an audience forgives.

So ownership is a row, and the guard is an index:

CREATE UNIQUE INDEX publishing_ledger_active_owner ON publishing_ledger (reel_id, platform) WHERE status IN ('claimed', 'scheduled', 'published');

Metricool claims (reel_id, platform). Buffer's run reaches the same pair and just INSERTs — no check first, on purpose. Postgres answers 23505 and the claim is refused.

It has to be the index, not a check-then-insert in application code. Two separate processes on separate schedules will lose that race, and a constraint is a refusal the caller cannot forget to handle.

It's partial so failed and cancelled release the pair for a retry, while published stays active — a published reel is still owned, or the other scheduler posts it again tomorrow.

Measured on the run: 12 owned pairs, 12 refused, 0 created. The duplicate never reached createPost.

A green test proves nothing.

You wrote the regression test. It passes. So does a test that asserts nothing at all — you can't tell those two apart from a green run.

The only proof is red. Revert the fix on purpose, run the same command, and watch it fail. Then put the fix back.

Real example: the regression test for a GraphQL input type only counts because reverting CreatePostInput! back to PostInput! turns it red. If it had stayed green with the fix removed, it was testing nothing and should be deleted, not kept for comfort.

A test you have not watched fail is not a test.

A reviewer that can edit is not a reviewer.

Omit the tools field on a subagent and it inherits every tool available. Name them and the field becomes an allowlist — only what's listed survives.

--- name: reviewer description: Reviews a diff. Reports, never edits. tools: Read, Grep, Glob ---

Everything unlisted is denied. You don't list anything to deny it.

This matters more than it sounds. A reviewer holding Write will quietly fix what it finds, and you'll never see the finding — you'll see a diff that grew while you weren't looking. No Bash either. Its only output should be the review.

captions.instagram:
editPost replaces the post. It does not patch it.

Moving a scheduled time looks like a one-field edit, so you send { id, dueAt } and expect everything else to stay put.

It doesn't. The omitted fields are cleared, not kept. All thirty edits came back refused — Invalid post: Post must have either text or media. — plus the per-platform complaints about a missing type and a missing title.

That refusal is the only reason nothing was damaged. An edit the API had ACCEPTED would have left thirty scheduled posts with no video in them, and nothing would have logged.

So rebuild the whole intended payload every time: text, assets, per-platform metadata, scheduling type, mode, and the scheduling fields. Never treat a replace-shaped mutation as a PATCH.
